label: Glass
summary: Panes, shelves, tubes, solar panel fronts and screens break into sharp fragments. Toughened glass can burst into small cubes with no warning, especially if its edge is chipped. Big panes are heavy and cut deep.
signs: Glass shelves, doors and oven windows
Large windows, display cases and mirrors
Fluorescent tubes, bulbs and CRT screens
Chips at the edges or corners of toughened glass
do: Wear gloves and eye protection when handling glass
Carry panes upright on edge, with a firm grip on both sides
Tape a cross over a cracked pane before moving it
Sweep up fragments and wrap them before throwing them away
Check floors and seats for splinters before kneeling or sitting
dont: Don't carry big panes flat, or in wind: they catch the air and flex
Don't try to catch a falling pane
Don't break glass with your hand or foot
Don't pick up fine splinters with bare fingers: use tape or a damp cloth
ppe: Cut-resistant gloves; thick leather helps but isn’t cut-resistant on its own
firstAid: Press firmly on a bleeding cut with a clean pad for at least 10 minutes
Rinse cuts with clean water and lift out loose surface splinters
Don't pull out a large or deep piece: pad around it and get medical help
Spurting blood, a gaping cut, or numbness or weakness below the cut needs real medical care

Glass in an eye: don't rub or press on it; rinse out loose specks with clean water; if a piece is stuck in the eye, leave it, cover the eye with a paper cup or shield without pressing, and get medical help

Heavy bleeding from an arm or leg that hard pressure can't stop: put a tourniquet (a wide strap tightened by twisting a stick) a hand's width above the wound, not on a joint, tighten until the bleeding stops, note the time, and get medical help
